item.title: Exercise 2: Documentation
item.dc:creator: pedro
item.description: Looking back at the documentation plan I wrote in Project 4, most of what I committed to is in place. The learning log has been updated at each significant stage. Email correspondence with Elena, John,...
item.content:encoded:
Looking back at the documentation plan I wrote in Project 4, most of what I committed to is in place. The learning log has been updated at each significant stage. Email correspondence with Elena, John, António has been kept and provides a detailed record of how decisions were made and who made them. Draft scores have been saved and dated throughout the process.

The main gap is direct observation of the students. The original plan assumed I would visit classes during the rehearsal period, but this did not happen until very late. I asked Elena on 28 May if I could attend a class, and she agreed immediately. She then asked the elementary principal whether I needed any permit or paperwork to visit. I am still waiting for that to be resolved. It means my record of how the students engaged with the material comes almost entirely from Elena’s reports in the email thread rather than from my own observation.

The email thread itself has turned out to be more useful documentation than I expected. It captures decisions in real time, including Elena’s revisions to the string parts, the third movement ending discussion, and António’s suggestion about the Portuguese text. These exchanges show the collaborative process more clearly than any summary I could write after the fact.

For the performance, the plan was to have it recorded on video. However, the school year ends on 25 June and it is now unlikely there will be a live performance. I am waiting for confirmation. If the performance does not go ahead, the primary documentation of the finished work will be the scores and the rehearsal process rather than a recording of the piece in front of an audience. This is an unexpected outcome, and one I will need to address in the evaluation.

Revised Project Timeline

January 2026 Initial planning phase. Pedro develops the concept and structural approach: a three-part piece built around a bridges metaphor covering past, present, and future. First discussions with Elena and John. The proposal is submitted to OCA.

February 2026 The original plan called for meetings with 5th grade students to understand their capabilities, and collaboration with Portuguese, history, and drama teachers. In practice, this phase was slower than planned. Direct contact with students did not happen. The collaboration remained primarily between Pedro, Elena, and John.

March 2026 Composition work begins. Pedro drafts the three movements. The minimalist, Glass-influenced structure of Part I takes shape. The bilingual dimension of the text is established, with Portuguese lines carrying emotional rather than translational weight.

April 2026 Composition continues. The aleatoric structure of Part III is developed, with the conductor activating each section’s 4-bar theme unpredictably. Elena begins advising on note ranges and what is feasible for 5th grade string players.

May 2026 (early) Elena revises the string parts significantly: simplifies to unison, lowers bass octaves, adds fingerings. Pedro sends revised Parts 1 and 3 on 25 May.

May 2026 (late) Elena does the first reading with her 5th graders on 28 May. Part I works well. Part II needs further simplification. Part III is manageable. High School orchestra students are enlisted to help with percussion and support the strings in Part II. Pedro asks to visit a class. Elena agrees immediately and refers the request for sign-off. Still pending.

June 2026 (early) António Andrade, the drama teacher, joins the email thread with a creative suggestion for the first time: changing “Nós construímos” to “Que construímos” in the dual-language sequence. Pedro accepts immediately. Elena sends final simplified scores. Rehearsals continue.

June 2026 (late) Performance date unconfirmed. School year ends 25 June. A live performance is now unlikely. Waiting for confirmation.

item.content:encoded:
The final weeks have been mostly about the score and the first readings with the students. A lot has happened in a short time.

Elena has taken real ownership of the string parts. Between 19 May and 28 May she revised them several times, simplifying to unison, lowering bass octaves, adding fingerings, and laying out parts across pages for readability. Some of these changes altered the music. I had written high Cs and As in the basses that simply do not work at this level, and she corrected them. When she reported back after the first reading with the 5th graders, the picture was mixed: the first movement worked well and the students learned staggered entrances; the second needed further simplification and she kept them in pizzicato; the third was fine.

Elena suggested treating the final section as a loop, leaving the conductor to decide whether the piece fades out or builds to a climax. I wrote back saying I liked the idea and wanted to frame it as a deliberate improvisatory choice. I have never done anything quite like this before and I am genuinely curious how it will work in performance.

The most surprising moment came on 2 June, when António Andrade sent a note about a single line in the dual-language sequence. The original read “We are the bridges / Nós construímos.” He suggested “Que construímos” instead. His explanation was careful: the first version creates two separate sentences, while the second fuses them into one thought that crosses between languages. He was right, and the change took two minutes to agree.

I have been thinking about that exchange quite a bit. It was the only moment in the whole project where someone challenged a creative decision on artistic grounds rather than practical ones. And it came from the person who was most peripheral to the process, almost at the last minute. I am not sure what to make of that yet, but it feels like something worth returning to when I write the evaluation.

I have also asked Elena if I can visit one of her classes before the performance, partly because I want to see the students working with the material, and partly because I need to document it for the university submission.
